q: 1. The increase in the strength of concrete with time is
explain: Concrete strength gain over time follows a non-linear curve — rapid initially and gradually slowing down, not a straight line.

q: 2. The test conducted in the laboratory on the specimen made out of trial concrete mix is called
explain: A preliminary test is conducted in the laboratory on trial mixes before actual construction to determine and verify the proportions needed to achieve the required strength.

q: 3. Di-calcium silicate (C2S)
options: provides less ultimate strength to cement
has less resistance to soleplate attack
explain: Dicalcium silicate (C2S) hydrates slowly and, correspondingly, releases less heat of hydration compared to tricalcium silicate.

q: 4. The ordinary concrete is not used for ......... grade of concrete mix.
explain: Ordinary (nominal mix) concrete is limited to lower/moderate grades; high-strength grades such as M40 require controlled mix design and are not made using ordinary concrete practice.

q: 5. The controlled concrete is used for
explain: Controlled concrete mix design is applicable across the full range of seven grades of concrete specified in the code.

q: 6. As the grade of concrete increases the quantity of cement required per cubic metre
explain: Higher grade concrete requires higher compressive strength, which is generally achieved by increasing the cement content per cubic metre of concrete.

q: 7. The bond strength between steel and concrete is due to
explain: The bond between reinforcing steel and surrounding concrete develops through a combination of both frictional resistance and adhesive chemical bonding at the interface.

q: 8. Pick up the incorrect statement from the following
options: workability of the concrete mix decreases with an increase in the moisture content
concrete for which preliminary tests are conducted, is called controlled concrete
bulking of sand depends upon the finesse of grains
concrete mix 1:6:12, is used for mass concrete in piers
explain: Workability actually increases (not decreases) with an increase in moisture content up to a point, since more water makes the mix more fluid and easier to work with, making this the incorrect statement.

q: 9. Poisson's ratio of concrete reduced by using
explain: Using a richer mix (more cement content) tends to reduce the Poisson's ratio of the resulting concrete.

q: 10. The durability of concrete is due to its resistance to
explain: Durability of concrete is defined by its overall ability to resist deterioration from a combination of environmental exposure, internal disruptive forces, and chemical attack/cracking.

q: 11. In concrete, use of angular crushed aggregate in place of natural rounded gravel affects
explain: as per book c.Angular crushed aggregate provides better mechanical interlock and bond with the cement matrix, which particularly improves the flexural tensile strength of the concrete.

q: 12. The cube strength of concrete exceeds the cylinder strength by (in percent)
explain: Due to the difference in specimen geometry and the resulting confinement/end effects during testing, cube strength typically exceeds cylinder strength by about 20 to 25%.

q: 13. The surface area of standard cube used for finding compressive strength of concrete is
explain: The standard cube face is 15cm x 15cm = 225 cm² = 22500 mm² = 0.0225 m² - all these are equivalent expressions of the same area in different units, so all of the above is correct.

q: 14. The ultimate load of a balanced reinforced concrete beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of concrete and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: In a balanced section, both the concrete's crushing (compressive) strength and the steel's tensile strength reach their limiting values simultaneously, so the ultimate load depends on both.

q: 15. The grade of concrete M 15 means that compressive strength of 15 cm cube after 28 days is
explain: By definition, the grade designation M150 directly specifies a characteristic compressive strength of 150 kg/cm² for a 15cm cube tested after 28 days.

q: 16. The standard size of a concrete cube for compressive strength test is
explain: The standard concrete cube specimen size used for compressive strength testing is 150 mm x 150 mm x 150 mm (15 cm cube).

q: 17. If the various concrete ingredients i.e. cement, sand and aggregates are in the ratio of 1:3:6, the grade of concrete, is
explain: The nominal mix ratio 1:3:6 corresponds to the M150 grade of concrete as per standard grade-mix ratio correlations.

q: 18. Permissible compressive strength of M150 concrete grade is
explain: 150 kg/cm² is equivalent to approximately 15 N/mm² (since 1 N/mm² ≈ 10.2 kg/cm²), making 15 N/mm² the correct equivalent expression of the M150 grade strength.

q: 19. Permissible compressive strength of M300 concrete grade is
explain: By definition, the M300 grade concrete has a characteristic (permissible) compressive strength of 300 kg/cm².

q: 20. The concrete mixes are designated into
explain: As per the classification used in this text (older IS 456 provisions), concrete mixes are designated into seven standard grades.

q: 21. For the construction of RCC slab, column, beam and walls, the minimum grade of concrete mixed is used for
explain: The minimum recommended nominal mix for general RCC construction (slabs, columns, beams, walls) is 1:2:4, corresponding to M15 grade concrete.

q: 22. M100 grade of concrete approximates
explain: The M100 grade of concrete (lowest strength grade) approximately corresponds to a lean nominal mix ratio of 1:3:6.

q: 23. The number of bags of cement required per cubic meter of 1:2:4 concrete will be approximately
explain: For a nominal 1:2:4 concrete mix, standard calculations show that approximately 4 to 5 bags of cement (50 kg each) are needed per cubic metre of concrete.

q: 24. The increase in strength of concrete after 6 months
explain: As per the strength-gain data referenced in this text, concrete strength increases by about 20% beyond the 28-day value after 6 months of curing.

q: 25. The modulus of elasticity E of concrete can be taken as
explain: As per IS 456, the static modulus of elasticity of concrete is commonly estimated using the empirical formula E = 5700√fck (in N/mm²).

q: 26. The concrete mix which causes difficulty in obtaining a smooth finish, possess
explain: A harsh concrete mix, characterized by excessive hardness/lack of fines, makes it difficult to achieve a smooth surface finish.

q: 27. The top diameter, bottom diameter, and the height of slump mould are
explain: As per IS 1199, the standard slump cone mould has a top diameter of 10 cm, bottom diameter of 20 cm, and a height of 30 cm.

q: 28. The grade of concrete not recommended by IS 456 is
explain: As per the classification referenced in this text, M30 does not appear among the listed standard grades recommended by IS 456.

q: 29. The preliminary test is repeated if the difference of compressive strength of three test specimen exceeds
explain: As per the acceptance criteria in this text, the preliminary test must be repeated if the difference in compressive strength among the three test specimens exceeds 15 kg/cm².

q: 30. For the construction of RCC slabs, columns, beams, walls etc, the grade of concrete mix used is
explain: For general RCC structural elements like slabs, columns, beams and walls, the nominal mix commonly used is 1:2:4 (equivalent to M15 grade).

q: 31. Generally nominal mix is done by volume while design mix is done by
explain: Design mixes require accurate proportioning of ingredients, which is achieved by batching materials by weight rather than the less precise volume batching used in nominal mixes.

q: 32. Ordinary concrete is not used for concrete grade
explain: Ordinary (nominal mix) concrete is only applicable to lower/moderate grades; higher grades like M40 require designed/controlled mix proportions and cannot use nominal mix ratios.

q: 33. If X, Y, Z are the fineness modulus of coarse, fine and combined aggregates, the percentage p of fine aggregates combined aggregate is
explain: As per the standard fineness-modulus blending formula used in this text, the percentage of fine aggregate in the combined aggregate is given by P = (X−Z)/(Z−Y) × 100, where X, Y, Z are the FM of coarse, fine, and combined aggregate respectively.

q: 34. The minimum grade of concrete for pre-tensioned member is
explain: Pre-tensioned members require high early strength to allow release of the tendons, so a minimum grade of M40 concrete is specified.

q: 35. The ferrocement is a composite material obtained by
options: random disposal of short, discontinuous fibres in the conventional concrete
reinforcing the cement mortar with steel fibres in the form of wire mesh
blending ferrous compounds in the ordinary Portland cement
explain: Ferrocement is defined as cement mortar reinforced with closely spaced layers of continuous, relatively thin steel wire mesh, distinguishing it from randomly dispersed fibre-reinforced concrete.

q: 36. The volume of reinforcement in ferrocement (percent) normally varies between
explain: In typical ferrocement construction, the volume fraction of the wire mesh reinforcement generally lies in the range of 5% to 8% of the total volume.

q: 37. The individual variation between test strength of sample should not be more than
explain: As per test acceptance criteria, the deviation of an individual test result from the average of the sample should not exceed ±15% of the average value.
